newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda genocide tribunal off to slow start.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide tribunal off to slow start.

text.p: The slow start of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, two years after the genocide of up to a million people, has fuelled fires lit by its critics.
In an unfinished Arusha courtroom with no witnesses set to testify and no Rwandan journalists present to see justice done, it last week postponed its first two trials for a second time.

The prosecution, defence and the tribunal were simply not ready, despite the three judges firing a public warning shot by initially threatening to resume Jean Paul Akayesu's trial on Monday before agreeing to put it off until the end of October.
Georges Rutaganda, one of four Rwandan Hutu accused held in Arusha, never even appeared in court as he is seriously ill and in a hospital. He secured a postponement until March next year.
Only the two defence lawyers, those accused of genocide and crimes against humanity in three months of mass slaughter in Rwanda and those still evading arrest had reason to be pleased.

It was a sorry conclusion, reinforcing worries that U.N. bureaucracy and the difficulties of operating from Tanzania would defeat the tribunal's ground-breaking moral mission that no one should be free to escape being judged for their crimes.
The new delays added to the immense frustration felt by Rwanda's government and relatives of the dead -- and fears that yet another U.N. operation in Africa was going horribly wrong.
But in their defence the tribunal judges, aware of the poor impression, are growing increasingly impatient and are staking their reputations on real progress being just round the corner.
They say the Rwanda tribunal was built from the ground up in this northern Tanzanian farming town and still worked faster than its sister tribunal on the former Yugoslavia in The Hague.
Asked what he could say to the still grieving relatives of the dead from the 1994 genocide who argued that justice delayed was no justice, Swedish Judge Lennart Aspegren told Reuters:
"I would like to say to them that they should know there are serious international efforts to have justice done. And this is something which is absolutely unique for Africa.
"It should be unique because the genocide in Rwanda as far as I know was the worst genocide we have ever heard about if you take into consideration it took place in a very few months."
"It is a slow and shaky start," conceded Judge Navanethem Pillay of South Africa, noting even judges complained about waiting for a year before being put on full-time duty with salaries.
"Everybody has legitimate complaints -- but this is a mammoth task and entirely new for Africa," she added.
"If you take a court system in a national state, everything is there: rules, buildings, experienced staff and equipment. But this thing had to be brought to Arusha and set up."
Not a single journalist from Rwanda was in court last week to tell Rwanda and the estimated 1.7 million Rwandan Hutu refugees outside the country the tribunal was even in session.
Officials said Rwandan journalists did not have the money to reach Arusha and transmit their stories or film and promised the tribunal would make more efforts to help them cover trials.
"It is highly relevant emotionally, psychologically for people inside Rwanda to know about the progress of the tribunal so they can begin the process of rebuilding their nation."

Rwandan Vice-President Paul Kagame, whose Tutsi-led rebels seized power in July 1994, and Zimbabwe's defence minister on Thursday accused the United Nations of racial bias, saying it was moving faster to bring Bosnian war criminals to justice.
Such accusations are patently untrue, Rwanda tribunal officials said, noting the former Yugoslavia tribunal had taken three years to bring its only suspect in custody to trial.
The Rwanda tribunal, with a budget of $36 million for 1996 which was only approved by the U.N. in June, has indicted 21 suspects of whom 11 are in custody, including four in Arusha.

Aspegren said the tribunal hit all kinds of problems imaginable, especially communications. In addition there are many problems peculiar to Rwanda, where potential witnesses are being attacked and threatened.
Because of insecurity, no tribunal investigator for the prosecution has visited Zaire, with 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus.
The tribunal last week ruled the identities of witnesses would be kept from the public and the media to protect them.
Witnesses will testify by camera from a room outside the courtroom. Only the judges will be able to see their faces.
"You can never of course have 100 percent security," admitted Aspegren. "(But) we are breaking new legal ground."
